# SGLang maps

Three maps of SGLang, each read from the source at commit b252aceffe (2026-09-27) and each
answering a different question.

| map | what it answers | in this folder |
|---|---|---|
| [SGLang Product Surface Requirements](https://claude.ai/artifact/Cx7SfSwGGVtzAgiUPNMLxw) | **What SGLang offers, and to whom.** Users and scope, the runtime's processes, every interface (CLI, about 90 HTTP routes, the Python `Engine`, two gRPC modes, the frontend language), 279 model architectures and 54 diffusion pipelines, generation and performance features, scale-out and the model gateway, nine hardware platforms, RL integration, operations, the configuration surface, code footprint, and open questions. | `product_surface.md`, `product_surface.pdf` |
| [How SGLang Works](https://claude.ai/artifact/BxQpeNsiXXzwrd7rz8X62C) | **How a request becomes GPU work.** The request lifecycle, the scheduler loop, memory and the KV cache, RadixAttention, model execution and the anatomy of a model, parallelism, prefill-decode disaggregation, speculative decoding, constrained decoding, LoRA and parsers, kernels, what sits beyond the LLM runtime, and a code map, all with file references. | `how_sglang_works.md`, `how_sglang_works.pdf` |
| [SGLang Config Space](https://claude.ai/artifact/M4TW6n2Biq8jSLHTghJYsy) | **Which knobs exist and what they are tied to.** Every server flag (515), gateway flag (93) and env var (648) laid on the inference stack from platform to fleet, with the 954 rules in the code that make one setting depend on another. | `config_space/` ([its README](config_space/README.md)) |

Read them in that order: the product surface is the outside view (what a user can call, run and
set), how it works is the inside view (the code paths behind it), and the config space sits
between the two (the settings that choose among those code paths). The product surface's
"Configuration surface" section is a summary; the config space map is the full version.

The accompanying principle, [The codebase has a shape, and so does the work on it](codebase_and_work_shape.md),
explains how these views can inform a map of changes: their preconditions, effects,
dependencies, and the obligations that make them admissible.

[The formalization](formal/README.md) writes these maps as Lean types: what SGLang does, what
interacts with what, and the operations on the codebase with which of them are admissible.
[The work study](work/FINDINGS.md) maps SGLang's last 100 commits and latest 500 issues onto a
vocabulary drawn from that model, with two independent labellers against criteria fixed in
advance, and asks whether the gaps it flags predicted regressions.

The [benchmark shape catalogues](benchmarks/README.md) apply that principle to SWE-bench's
12 core codebases, all 278 tasks in a pinned τ²-bench release, and 155 tasks across
Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 2.1. They connect each shape to admissible operations, validation
methods, and a proposed experiment for measuring whether project-specific harnesses help.

[An agent organized as a nested graph of skills](skill_graph/README.md) develops the next
step: reusable methods, parameterized contracts, Lean-checked composition, and separate
go/no-go tests for the skill graph and for the value of formalizing it.

## Live pages and the copies here

The links above are the current versions. The first two are living docs, so they can move on
after the copies here were taken.

- `*.md` are exports of the docs taken on 2026-09-27: the full text, with each diagram (2 in the
  product surface, 6 in how it works) replaced by a pointer to the PDF and the live doc.
- `*.pdf` are exports from the same day with the diagrams drawn; one diagram in
  `how_sglang_works.pdf` came out as text.
- `config_space/config_space.html` is the published page itself, generated from the code by
  `config_space/src/`. It deep-links to any knob by id, for example
  `config_space.html#l5.pool.page-size`. To rebuild it after the code moves:

      cd maps/config_space
      python3 src/extract.py    # re-read flags, env vars and rules from this checkout
      python3 src/build.py      # validate and write config_space.html

## Related maps

These three cover SGLang itself. The [Inference Optimization Map](https://claude.ai/artifact/Ppy99C282sgbCktwTkivwr)
covers 607 inference optimization techniques across the field. [The Compute Stack](https://claude.ai/artifact/5Ui8o6yktLeYu5qBscGqnd)
is the stack model the config space borrows its layers from.

1	# The shape of SGLang, and of the work on it
2	
3	The general statement is `../codebase_and_work_shape.md`. This document applies it to SGLang,
4	concretely, and names the terms the Lean in this folder uses.
5	
6	A codebase is not a bag of files, and work on it is not a bag of diffs. SGLang has a
7	shape: layers that read each other in one direction, components that sit at one layer
8	each, typed interactions between them, registries where the code says "one of these",
9	invariants that hold across all of it, and gates that say who may change what. Work on
10	the codebase has a shape too: every change is an operation on that structure, with a
11	footprint, a reach, preconditions and obligations. Two diffs of the same size can be
12	operations of different kinds, and some operations are not admissible at all. This
13	document says what that means in detail; the rest of the folder makes it precise.
14	
15	## 1. The shape of the codebase
16	
17	### 1.1 Layers
18	
19	The config-space map lays SGLang on seven layers, bottom to top: platform, model and
20	numerics, kernels and collectives, parallelism and execution, memory and KV cache,
21	scheduling and decoding, serving and fleet. The layers are ordered: a layer reads the
22	layers below it and is read by the layers above. The GPU is decided at layer 1 and
23	everything above branches on it (165 of the 954 coupling rules branch on hardware); the
24	model is decided at layer 2 and 197 rules branch on it. Nothing at layer 3 knows what a
25	request is; nothing at layer 7 knows what a slot is.
26	
27	### 1.2 Components
28	
29	A component is a named part of the runtime that lives at one layer and in one or two
30	files: the tokenizer manager, the scheduler, the prefill adder, the request-to-token
31	pool, the radix tree, the model runner, the attention backend, the KV sender, the EAGLE
32	worker, the grammar manager, the model gateway. The inventory names 82.
33	A component is the unit at which the shape is drawn: interactions connect components,
34	knobs configure components, operations touch components.
35	
36	### 1.3 Interactions
37	
38	An interaction is a typed edge between two components. The type matters more than the
39	edge, because the type says what breaks when either end changes:
40	
41	| kind | meaning | example |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| sends | a message crosses a process boundary | tokenizer manager → scheduler, `TokenizedGenerateReqInput` over ZMQ |
44	| calls | an in-process call with a contract | scheduler → model runner, `forward(ForwardBatch)` |
45	| owns | one side allocates or holds what the other uses | radix tree owns cached KV slots; requests own only a partial last page |
46	| reads / writes | shared state, no call | attention backend writes K and V into the KV pool at pre-allocated slots |
47	| transfers | bulk data moves between servers | prefill KV sender → decode KV receiver, one-sided RDMA |
48	| replaces | one component stands in for another | the speculative worker replaces the scheduler's model worker |
49	| selects | a knob or auto-detection picks one alternative at a registry | `--attention-backend`, or the platform hook picking FA3 on Hopper |
50	| constrains | one knob's value limits another's | `--dcp-size > 1` with HiCache requires an MLA model |
51	
52	The batch chain `Req → ScheduleBatch → ForwardBatch` is three components joined by
53	calls, and the contract "`ForwardBatch.init_new` never mutates its input" is a property
54	of that edge, not of either end. The overlap scheduler exists because of one edge: the
55	GPU-side `FutureMap` lets batch N+1 read batch N's tokens without a CPU round trip.
56	
57	### 1.4 Registries and choice points
58	
59	A registry is a place where the code holds a set of alternatives and something picks
60	one: 24 attention backends, 31 quantization methods, 19 MoE runners, 8 speculative
61	algorithms, 9 scheduling policies, 5 eviction policies, 13 HiCache storage backends,
62	6 PD transfer backends, 41 tool-call parsers, 33 reasoning parsers, 18 load formats,
63	279 model architectures, 9 platforms. Each registry has five parts, and an alternative
64	is only fully added when all five agree:
65	
66	1. the registration (a dict, a decorator, an `EntryClass`, an entry point, a subclass);
67	2. the choice list the flag parser validates against (`arg_groups/choices.py`);
68	3. the capability declarations (which platforms, MLA or not, CUDA-graph capturable,
69	   deterministic, draft-capable, chunked-prefix capable);
70	4. the compatibility rules in the `arg_groups/*_hook.py` files that refuse or rewrite
71	   combinations;
72	5. the documentation and the tests that enumerate the alternatives.
73	
74	The registries are where the codebase is designed to grow. They are also where the
75	config space comes from.
76	
77	### 1.5 The config space is the free part of the shape
78	
79	Every one of the 515 server flags, 93 gateway flags and 648 environment variables is
80	either the selector of a registry (`--attention-backend`, `--moe-runner-backend`) or a
81	numeric or boolean parameter of one component (`--page-size` of the allocator,
82	`--chunked-prefill-size` of the prefill adder, `--hicache-size` of the host tier). So a
83	knob has a home: the component it parameterizes. The config-space map filed every knob
84	under one group of one layer; that filing is the home relation.
85	
86	The 954 rules are then not a separate fact about configuration. A rule couples two
87	knobs because their home components interact: `--page-size` and
88	`--disaggregation-mode` are coupled because prefill and decode servers must agree on
89	paging before KV can be written across them; `--speculative-algorithm` and
90	`--attention-backend` are coupled because the draft worker needs a backend that can
91	verify a tree. Given the components and their interactions, the config space is
92	implicit: it is the product of the components' parameters, and the rules are the
93	compatibility relation that the interactions induce on that product. That is why
94	this formalization does not model the config space as a thing of its own. Knobs appear
95	as fields of components; rules appear as constraints between fields whose owners are
96	connected.
97	
98	### 1.6 Invariants
99	
100	An invariant is a property of the whole shape that every admissible operation must
101	preserve. The maps and the repository's own tests name these, among others:
102	
103	- Every flag is declared in exactly one namespace class under `arg_groups/fields/`, and
104	  the projected config bags cover the fields exactly (`test_server_args_namespaces.py`).
105	- `ServerArgs` is never written after resolution; decisions are read from the bags, and
106	  the read and mutation ratchets are pinned at zero.
107	- Every rule names only flags that exist, and every resolution rule writes a flag that
108	  some group owns.
109	- Every alternative in a choice list is registered, and every registered alternative
110	  that a flag can select is in the choice list.
111	- Every KV slot is owned by exactly one of: the free list, a request's partial last
112	  page, or the radix tree; locked tokens are protected, unlocked leaves are evictable.
113	- Both sides of a prefill-decode pair use the same page size and KV dtype.
114	- `max_running_requests` is bounded by the request-to-token pool's rows; admission
115	  charges every request against the three prefill budgets.
116	- The batch chain is `Req → ScheduleBatch → ForwardBatch`, and `init_new` does not
117	  mutate its input.
118	- A model's recommended deployment lives on its cookbook page, and changes that alter
119	  it change the page in the same PR.
120	
121	### 1.7 Gates
122	
123	A gate is a rule about who may change what, and how. The repository states its gates
124	in `.claude/rules/` and `.claude/skills/`: `model_runner.py` is frozen and
125	orchestration-only; the `__init__` of `Scheduler`, `TokenizerManager` and `ModelRunner`
126	is a sequence of `init_*` helpers; speculative-decoding identifiers follow six naming
127	rules; environment variables are `SGLANG_*` descriptors on the `Envs` class with a verb
128	category; kernels are placed by computation in an `ops` group and registered with
129	`KernelSpec` metadata; module-level globals in the flag-owning layers are pinned by
130	name. Gates are not invariants of the runtime; they are invariants of the codebase as an
131	artifact people work on. They are part of the shape all the same.
132	
133	## 2. The shape of the work
134	
135	### 2.1 An operation is a typed transformation, not a diff
136	
137	A diff is text. An operation is what the diff does to the shape: which registry it
138	extends, which knob it adds, which edge it rewires, which invariant it touches. The same
139	operation can be spelled as many diffs, and one diff can carry several operations. The
140	useful unit of review, testing and approval is the operation.
141	
142	Operations fall into classes, ordered roughly by how far they reach:
143	
144	| class | what it does to the shape | footprint |
145	|---|---|---|
146	| extension | adds an alternative at a registry | the registry's five parts |
147	| parameterization | adds, renames, deprecates a knob, or changes its default | the knob's home, every rule naming it, every cookbook page setting it |
148	| coupling | adds or changes a rule | the knobs named and the hook file |
149	| surface | adds a route, an interface, a CLI command | the entry point and the request path behind it |
150	| mechanism | changes how one component works inside | the component and its neighbours through the edges it exposes |
151	| rewiring | changes an interaction: a transport, an owner, a hop | both endpoints and everything that assumed the old edge |
152	| structural | changes an invariant | the closure of everything that relied on it |
153	| policy | changes a gate | every future operation of the gated kind |
154	
155	An extension at a well-designed registry is local by construction: adding the 42nd
156	tool-call parser touches the parser registry, the choice list and a docs table. A
157	structural change is cross-cutting by construction: changing what a page means touches
158	the allocator, the radix tree, HiCache's page hashing, both PD sides, FA3's page table,
159	chunk alignment in the prefill adder and every attention backend's index gathering.
160	
161	### 2.2 Footprint, affected, consulted, obligations, gates
162	
163	Each operation has measurable properties, none of them the line count:
164	
165	- **Footprint**: the components it edits.
166	- **Affected**: the components whose existing behaviour can change, what a deployment that
167	  does nothing new would notice. A new alternative, knob or rule that nobody selects affects
168	  nothing yet; a changed default, a removal, a mechanism or a rewired edge affects what every
169	  deployment runs, through the interactions and the rules.
170	- **Consulted**: the components whose rules must now account for the change. A new attention
171	  backend affects nothing, but every rule that branches on `--attention-backend` (homed in 20
172	  components) must decide whether the new value is compatible.
173	- **Layers crossed**: the layers the affected components span.
174	- **Obligations**: the in-codebase invariants the change *preserves* (those the affected
175	  components can break) and the ones it *takes on* (the contract of the registry a new
176	  alternative joins, or the invariant a structural change rewrites).
177	- **Gates**: the on-codebase rules the operation must pass.
178	
179	A single "radius" conflates affected and consulted, and makes an extension look as large as a
180	change of default. The split is what explains why extensions are cheap: they affect nothing,
181	though they must be consulted about and must honour a contract.
182	
183	These are computable from the shape. The most coupled knobs in the catalog say where
184	operations are expensive before anyone opens a file: `model_path` appears in 149 rules,
185	`attention_backend` in 75, `disaggregation_mode` in 72, `tp_size` in 70,
186	`speculative_algorithm` in 65, `cuda_graph_config` in 61. A parameterization of any of
187	these is a large operation whatever its diff looks like.
188	
189	## 3. Not every operation is equal
190	
191	Two operations that each change thirty lines can differ by two orders of magnitude in what
192	they affect. Adding a tool-call parser affects nothing and needs CPU tests; changing
193	`page_size`'s default affects 28 components across all seven layers and needs multi-node
194	runs, benchmarks and the cookbook. Neither measure agrees with line count. Consequences follow from the
195	class and the measures, not from the diff:
196	
197	- how deep the review goes and who must be in it;
198	- which tests must run: one registry's tests, one layer's, or the platforms matrix;
199	- whether documentation must change, and which pages;
200	- whether the change can be a single commit or must be a relocation commit followed by
201	  a semantic commit (the kernel-organization rule);
202	- whether it can ship behind a flag or must land whole (rerouting a config writer
203	  means flipping all its readers in the same commit; no dual-write).
204	
205	Extensions are cheap because the registries were built to absorb them. Structural
206	changes are expensive because invariants are shared. Treating the two alike, in either
207	direction, is the mistake this principle exists to prevent.
208	
209	## 4. Not every operation is admissible
210	
211	An operation is admissible when it is well-typed, its preconditions hold, its
212	postcondition preserves the invariants, and its gates are discharged. Each of the four
213	fails in a different way.
214	
215	**Ill-typed.** The operation cannot be stated in the shape. An attention backend with no
216	platform list; a flag with no namespace; a rule naming a flag that does not exist; an
217	alternative for a registry that has no selector. A type system rejects these before any
218	reasoning about consequences.
219	
220	**Precondition failed.** The operation is stated but the codebase is not in the state
221	it needs. Adding a backend whose name is already in the choice list; deprecating a flag
222	that a cookbook page still sets; adding a resolution rule that writes a flag no group
223	owns.
224	
225	**Invariant broken.** The operation would leave the shape inconsistent. A backend in
226	the choice list but not in the registry, or registered but absent from the deterministic
227	list it claims to belong to; a prefill-decode pair that disagrees on page size; a write
228	to `ServerArgs` after publish; a fourth level in the batch chain that `init_new` would
229	have to mutate.
230	
231	**Gate not discharged.** The operation is consistent but the policy forbids it as
232	stated. Domain logic added to `model_runner.py`; a spec-decoding identifier named
233	`num_accepted_tokens`; a new `os.getenv("SGLANG_...")` call site; a kernel file placed
234	directly under `ops/`; a default change that alters a recommended deployment without
235	its cookbook page.
236	
237	The first three failures, and the gates a static check can see, are decidable on the shape:
238	given the current registries, knobs, rules and gates, each condition is checked. An
239	inadmissible operation is not a matter of taste; no evidence can rescue it. What the shape
240	cannot decide are the invariants in the codebase: whether a new backend really writes KV only
241	at its allocated slots. Those become obligations with named evidence, and until the evidence is
242	supplied the operation is *unestablished*: not refused, not yet shown valid. The Lean keeps the
243	three verdicts apart, and proves that refusal does not depend on evidence.
244	
245	## 5. What the formalization buys
246	
247	Writing the shape as types and data makes four things checkable that were previously
248	prose:
249	
250	1. **Construction**: an operation is a term of `Op`; one that is ill-typed for the shape (a
251	   plugin extension through a CLI-only adder, a knob whose group has no home) is refused
252	   before anything else is considered.
253	2. **Measurement**: footprint, affected, consulted, layers and evidence cost are functions of
254	   the operation, the interactions and the rules, computed rather than estimated.
255	3. **Admissibility**: preconditions, the on-codebase invariants and the decidable gates are
256	   decided on the catalog; that an admissible verdict preserves them is proved for every
257	   shape and operation.
258	4. **The config space for free**: knobs are fields of components and rules are
259	   constraints between connected components, so the 954-rule coupling graph is a
260	   derived object, not a separate model.
261	
262	The model is at the granularity of the maps: components, edges, registries, knobs and
263	rules, not functions and lines. It does not prove the runtime correct. Its facts come
264	from the three maps and the extracted catalog at commit b252aceffe, and it is wrong
265	wherever they are.
266	
267	## 6. Vocabulary
268	
269	| term | meaning |
270	|---|---|
271	| layer | one of seven horizontal bands; reads below, read from above |
272	| component | a named part at one layer, in one or two files |
273	| interaction | a typed edge between components (sends, calls, owns, reads, writes, transfers, replaces, selects, constrains) |
274	| registry | a set of alternatives with a selector and compatibility rules |
275	| alternative | one member of a registry |
276	| selector | the knob or the auto-detection that picks an alternative |
277	| knob | a server flag, gateway flag or env var; has a home component |
278	| rule | a constraint (refusal) or resolution (default rewrite) over knobs |
279	| invariant | a property of the whole shape every operation must preserve |
280	| gate | a policy about who may change what, and how |
281	| operation | a typed transformation of the shape |
282	| footprint | the components an operation edits |
283	| affected | the components whose existing behaviour it can change |
284	| consulted | the components whose rules must account for it |
285	| inadmissible | refused: ill-typed, a failed precondition, a broken on-codebase invariant, a prohibition |
286	| unestablished | not refused, but the evidence its obligations name is missing |
287	| admissible | not refused, and every named evidence supplied |
288	
289	The process the rest of this folder follows: `INVENTORY.md` notes down everything;
290	`INTERACTIONS.md` notes down what interacts with what; `SGLang/*.lean` defines the
291	types; `SGLang/Operations.lean` defines the operations and decides admissibility.

1	# SGLang, formalized
2	
3	The three maps of SGLang (`../README.md`) as Lean 4 types and data: what SGLang does and how,
4	what interacts with what, and what can be done to the codebase. The configuration space is not
5	modelled as a thing of its own; knobs are fields of components and rules are constraints
6	between them. The principle is `../codebase_and_work_shape.md`; `PRINCIPLE.md` applies it to
7	SGLang and defines the terms the Lean uses.
8	
9	The process, in order:
10	
11	1. **Note down everything**: `INVENTORY.md`. Layers, processes, components, registries,
12	   capabilities, mechanisms, gates, invariants.
13	2. **Note down what interacts with what**: `INTERACTIONS.md`. 168 hand-written typed edges,
14	   plus the `constrains` edges derived from the 954 rules.
15	3. **Define types for it**: `SGLang/*.lean`.
16	4. **Define the operations on the codebase, and which are admissible**: `SGLang/Operations.lean`,
17	   checked in `SGLang/Checks.lean`.
18	
19	## Files
20	
21	| file | what it holds |
22	|---|---|
23	| `SGLang/Stack.lean` | `Layer` (7), `Process` (8), `Component` (82, one layer each, with its path and processes) |
24	| `SGLang/Config.lean` | `Knob`, `Rule`, `Group` and the home relation: which component a knob parameterizes |
25	| `SGLang/Catalog.lean` | generated: every server flag (515), gateway flag (93), env var (648), rule (954), and the choice lists `server_arguments.mdx` prints |
26	| `SGLang/Choices.lean` | the alternatives at each choice point, with capabilities (platforms, deterministic, MLA, draft-capable) and defaults |
27	| `SGLang/Interactions.lean` | the hand-written edges: kind, boundary (in-process, IPC, network), provenance |
28	| `SGLang/Registry.lean` | 30 registries; each one's code, parser and docs lists, and the sync check between them |
29	| `SGLang/Coupling.lean` | derived `constrains` edges: rules pulled up from knobs to components |
30	| `SGLang/Obligations.lean` | invariants in the codebase (17) with their evidence; gates on it (24) with their source and what discharges them; `Evidence` and its cost |
31	| `SGLang/Operations.lean` | `Shape`, `Op` (15 constructors in 9 classes), footprint, affected, consulted, preserves, takes on, gates, evidence, refusals, `Verdict`, sequences, work orders |
32	| `SGLang/Checks.lean` | the theorems |
33	| `src/gen_catalog.py` | regenerates `Catalog.lean` from `../config_space/data/config_space.json` and `docs/docs/advanced_features/server_arguments.mdx` |
34	
35	## Building
36	
37	    python3 src/gen_catalog.py     # after the config-space map is rebuilt, or the docs change
38	    lake build                     # typechecks everything and decides every theorem
39	    lake exe sglang_formal         # prints the report: sync issues, couplings, work orders
40	
41	Lean v4.33.0, no dependencies.
42	
43	## What an operation gets
44	
45	Each operation is decided on the current shape and returns a work order:
46	
47	| field | meaning |
48	|---|---|
49	| class | extension, parameterization, coupling, surface, mechanism, rewiring, structural, policy, relocation |
50	| footprint | the components it edits |
51	| affected | components whose existing behaviour can change: what a deployment doing nothing new would notice |
52	| consulted | components whose rules must now account for it (for a new backend: every rule that branches on its selector) |
53	| preserves | in-codebase invariants it can break for existing deployments |
54	| takes on | invariants it becomes answerable for (a new alternative takes on its registry's contract) |
55	| gates | on-codebase rules it must pass |
56	| evidence | what establishes its obligations and discharges its gates, with a cost from 1 (seconds on a CPU) to 6 (the platform matrix) |
57	| refusals | why it cannot be right: ill-typed, a failed precondition, a broken invariant on the codebase, a prohibition |
58	
59	The verdict keeps the principle's distinction between *invalid* and *not yet established*:
60	`inadmissible` (a refusal, which no evidence fixes), `unestablished` (nothing refuses it,
61	evidence missing), `admissible`.
62	
63	## What is proved, what is decided, what is assumed
64	
65	- **Proved for every shape and operation** (`Checks.lean` §1): an admissible verdict leaves the
66	  codebase well formed and adds no registry-sync issue; refusal does not depend on evidence;
67	  supplying the required evidence settles an unrefused operation; a full in-tree extension
68	  never creates a sync issue.
69	- **Decided on the catalog at b252aceffe** (`Checks.lean` §2–3), with `native_decide`, which
70	  trusts Lean's compiler: the current codebase is well formed; 44 registry-sync issues exist;
71	  half-registrations and CLI-only plugin extensions are refused; order of removal matters;
72	  operations differ in affected components, layers and evidence cost.
73	- **Judgement, written by hand and marked**: component boundaries, the group-to-component and
74	  knob-to-component homes, invariant-to-component maps, registry contracts, evidence per
75	  invariant. Where the maps did not say, the Lean says `inferred`.
76	- **Not modelled**: what happens inside a component. A `changeMechanism` is never refused on
77	  the shape except where a gate says so; the model says which invariants it can reach and what
78	  would establish them.
79	
80	## Findings the checks surfaced
81	
82	- `server_arguments.mdx` has drifted from the code: 37 alternatives are undocumented across
83	  attention, linear attention, quantization, KV dtype, MoE runner and all-to-all, schedule and
84	  eviction policy, HiCache storage, load format and the parsers; `marlin` is documented but is
85	  not a quantization choice.
86	- The gateway's `bucket` and `consistent_hashing` policies cannot be selected in the Rust binary.
87	- Speculative algorithm, tool-call parser, reasoning parser and device have no parser choice
88	  list; an unknown value is refused, if at all, at run time.
89	- Only the two parser registries have a CI test tying choice list to registry.
90	- Six `add_*_choices` adders are CLI-only: FP8 GEMM, FP4 GEMM, PD transfer, load format,
91	  radix eviction, linear-attention kernel. A plugin using them gets past argparse and fails at
92	  run time.
93	- 236 of 269 derived coupling pairs have no drawn interaction in the how-it-works map; the
94	  heaviest are expert parallelism with the parallel topology (47 rules) and the MoE runner with
95	  quantization (29).

# Part C result: map-guided review against plain review (SGLang, at `b252aceffe`)

**Result: no measurable advantage for the map-guided method. Both methods found real, mostly unreported defects at about the same rate
(M1 map-guided: 19 reported, 19 real; M2 plain review: 23 reported, 22 real), each found a different half of the 28 distinct real defects, and the
map-guided reviewers said themselves that the site lists did not lead them to their findings.** Sample: two runs per method; this is one comparison
and small, so read the spread rather than the point values.

Defects found here are **not** reported upstream or fixed; they are listed below for the owner.

## Setup

- M1 (map-guided): `SITES.md`, `data/unguarded_head.json` (the finders' unguarded sites), the map documents (how-it-works, product surface,
  inventory, interactions, the abort behaviour model). M2 (plain review): repository only, `maps/` forbidden. Same model (the session model), same
  scope (whole repository), cap 150 tool calls (all four runs stopped earlier: harness-counted tool uses 63, 79 for M1 and 73, 75 for M2), no `gh`,
  no findings from earlier rounds, no issue tracker.
- Reports pooled (42 claims), shuffled and given neutral ids (`data/partC_pool.json`, key in `data/partC_key.json`), judged by a third subagent
  blind to method: real / not real / unsure, severity, already known, duplicate clusters (`tmp/adjC/verdicts.json`). The adjudicator used up to 40
  read-only `gh` calls, scanning about 3,000 recent issues and PRs, so "not known" is a weak statement.

## Numbers

| | M1 map-guided (2 runs) | M2 plain review (2 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| defects reported | 19 (11 + 8) | 23 (14 + 9) |
| judged real (precision) | 19 (100%) | 22 (96%) |
| distinct real defects (duplicate clusters) | 15 | 17 |
| of those, already known (tracker, or earlier rounds) | 3 | 2 |
| **latent (real, not known)** | **12** | **15** |
| found by this method only | 11 | 13 |
| harness-counted tool calls (two runs) | 142 | 148 |
| real per 100 calls | 13.4 | 14.9 |
| distinct real per 100 calls | 10.6 | 11.5 |

The union is **28 distinct real defects** (29 clusters, one not real): 4 found by both methods, 11 by M1 only, 13 by M2 only. Per run: M1
11 real / 11 distinct and 8 / 8; M2 13 / 12 and 9 / 9.

"Known" here: `#41474` (abort by rid prefix; found by both methods), `#41372` (stop-string decoded text), and the `/server_info` secret exposure,
which the tracker check did not match but which is `#37457`, reported in round 1 (both methods rediscovered it, and both wrote it up as a new
defect).

Classes of the claims (by the reviewer's own label): M1: other 7, default-swallow 3, secret-exposure 2, copy-drift 2, one each of terminal-leak,
weak-oracle, check-then-act, accepted-not-honored, fault-uncontained. M2: check-then-act 4, accepted-not-honored 3, secret-exposure 3,
fault-uncontained 3, cancel-window 2, copy-drift 2, other 2, one each of ordering-assumed, terminal-leak, default-swallow, unit-mismatch.
Twelve of 42 claims fit none of the seed classes ("other"); the interesting finds were mostly missing auth decorators, path handling and
API-edge validation, which the seed classes do not name (see `CLASS_PROPOSALS.md`).

## What the map did and did not do

- M1's own reports: "most of the SITES.md leads did not hold up" (run 1: the cancel-window sites had cleanup paths) and "only one defect fits
  the map's classes, found by reading code directly" (run 2). The finders' unguarded lists were used as leads and mostly rejected after reading.
  That matches their measured precision (0 to 80%).
- The map gave no visible advantage in breadth (11 vs 13 unique defects) or in yield per call.
- Overlap between methods is small (4 of 28), which means either method alone misses most of what the other finds; the sum of both was more
  useful than the better one. That is a statement about how sparse review coverage is, not about the map.

## Caveats

- Two runs per method; per-run counts range from 8 to 14. No significance test would mean anything at this size.

{"arguments":{"content":"/-!
# Behaviour: protocols as transition systems

The other modules draw SGLang's shape: components, edges, registries, operations. This one models what runs:
processes exchanging messages. It is written in the style of TLA+ (states, the actions enabled in a state, a
step function) but in Lean, so the whole map stays in one language. Every interleaving of enabled actions is a
behaviour, and there are three ways to use one:

- **explore** it breadth first to a bound, and print the first trace that breaks a property, as TLC would;
- **prove** a property for every reachable state with an inductive invariant, which TLC cannot do;
- **recast liveness as safety** where it matters: "once nothing is in flight, nothing is left running for a
  departed client" is a property of quiescent states.

The first protocol is request abort between the TokenizerManager and the scheduler. The reported bug (#36333;
see `maps/work/retro/REPORT_B.md`, where the link to 71043b9dbb is marked doubtful): on client disconnect the
TokenizerManager dropped the state of a request it had already dispatched, without sending `AbortReq`, so the
scheduler kept decoding for a client that was gone.
-/

namespace SGLang.Behaviour

/-! ## Transition systems -/

/-- Initial states, the actions enabled in a state, and what each action does. -/
structure System (σ α : Type) where
  init : List σ
  enabled : σ → List α
  step : σ → α → σ

/-- `s` is reached from an initial state by enabled actions, in some interleaving. -/
inductive Reachable (sys : System σ α) : σ → Prop
  | init {s : σ} : s ∈ sys.init → Reachable sys s
  | step {s : σ} {a : α} : Reachable sys s → a ∈ sys.enabled s → Reachable sys (sys.step s a)

/-- An invariant that holds initially and survives every enabled action holds in every reachable state. -/
theorem Reachable.inductive_invariant {sys : System σ α} (P : σ → Prop)
    (h0 : ∀ s, s ∈ sys.init → P s) (h1 : ∀ s a, P s → a ∈ sys.enabled s → P (sys.step s a)) :
    ∀ s, Reachable sys s → P s := by
  intro s hs
  induction hs with
  | init h => exact h0 _ h
  | step _ ha ih => exact h1 _ _ ih ha

/-- Breadth-first exploration to `depth` steps, keeping the first (shortest) trace that reaches each state. -/
def System.explore [BEq σ] (sys : System σ α) (depth : Nat) : List (List α × σ) :=
  go depth (sys.init.map fun s => ([], s)) (sys.init.map fun s => ([], s))
where
  go : Nat → List (List α × σ) → List (List α × σ) → List (List α × σ)
    | 0, seen, _ => seen
    | n + 1, seen, frontier =>
      let next := frontier.flatMap fun (tr, s) => (sys.enabled s).map fun a => (tr ++ [a], sys.step s a)
      let fresh := next.foldl (fun acc p => if (seen ++ acc).any (·.2 == p.2) then acc else acc ++ [p]) []
      if fresh.isEmpty then seen else go n (seen ++ fresh) fresh

/-- The shortest trace, within `depth` steps, to a state where `ok` fails. -/
def System.counterexample [BEq σ] (sys : System σ α) (ok : σ → Bool) (depth : Nat) : Option (List α × σ) :=
  (sys.explore depth).find? fun p => !ok p.2

/-! ## Request abort: TokenizerManager and scheduler -/

inductive Act where
  | submit      -- the TokenizerManager registers the request and sends `GenerateReq`
  | deliver     -- the scheduler receives the next message in flight
  | finish      -- the scheduler finishes decoding on its own (length or stop)
  | disconnect  -- the client goes away and the TokenizerManager reacts
deriving DecidableEq, Repr, BEq

/-- One request's state across both processes. Messages share one ordered channel, and `GenerateReq` is always
sent before any `AbortReq`, so two flags describe what is in flight. -/
structure St where
  client : Bool         -- the client is connected
  tmHas : Bool          -- the TokenizerManager holds the request's state
  dispatched : Bool     -- `GenerateReq` has been sent
  genInFlight : Bool    -- `GenerateReq` sent, not yet received
  abortInFlight : Bool  -- `AbortReq` sent, not yet received
  running : Bool        -- the scheduler is decoding the request
  done : Bool           -- the scheduler finished or aborted it
deriving DecidableEq, Repr, BEq

def start : St := ⟨true, false, false, false, false, false, false⟩

def enabled (s : St) : List Act :=
  (if s.client && !s.dispatched then [.submit] else []) ++
  (if s.genInFlight || s.abortInFlight then [.deliver] else []) ++
  (if s.running then [.finish] else []) ++
  (if s.client then [.disconnect] else [])

/-- The scheduler takes the oldest message: a request starts unless already finished; an abort stops it. -/
def receive (s : St) : St :=
  if s.genInFlight then { s with genInFlight := false, running := !s.done }
  else if s.abortInFlight then { s with abortInFlight := false, running := false, done := true }
  else s

def stepWith (onDisconnect : St → St) (s : St) : Act → St
  | .submit => { s with tmHas := true, dispatched := true, genInFlight := true }
  | .deliver => receive s
  | .finish => { s with running := false, done := true }
  | .disconnect => onDisconnect s

/-- The protocol as intended: dropping a dispatched request's state first sends `AbortReq`. -/
def disconnectFixed (s : St) : St :=
  { s with client := false, tmHas := false, abortInFlight := s.abortInFlight || (s.tmHas && s.dispatched) }

/-- The reported bug: the state of a dispatched request is discarded and the scheduler is never told. -/
def disconnectBuggy (s : St) : St :=
  { s with client := false, tmHas := false }

def fixed : System St Act := ⟨[start], enabled, stepWith disconnectFixed⟩
def buggy : System St Act := ⟨[start], enabled, stepWith disconnectBuggy⟩

/-- No zombie: while the scheduler decodes for a departed client, an `AbortReq` is on its way. -/
def noZombie (s : St) : Bool := !(!s.client && s.running && !s.abortInFlight)

/-- Liveness recast as safety: once nothing is in flight, nothing decodes for a departed client. -/
def quiescentClean (s : St) : Bool := !(!s.genInFlight && !s.abortInFlight && !s.client && s.running)

/-! ### The buggy protocol: a counterexample, found and then stated -/

/-- Exploration finds the three-step trace: dispatch, start decoding, client leaves. -/
theorem buggy_counterexample :
    (buggy.counterexample noZombie 8).map (·.1) = some [.submit, .deliver, .disconnect] := by
  native_decide

/-- The same trace as a proof that the buggy protocol reaches a zombie. -/
theorem buggy_reaches_zombie : ∃ s, Reachable buggy s ∧ noZombie s = false := by
  have h0 : Reachable buggy start := .init (by simp [buggy])
  have h1 : Reachable buggy (buggy.step start .submit) := .step h0 (by decide)
  have h2 : Reachable buggy (buggy.step (buggy.step start .submit) .deliver) := .step h1 (by decide)
  exact ⟨_, .step (a := .disconnect) h2 (by decide), by decide⟩

/-! ### The fixed protocol: bounded check, then a proof for every reachable state -/

theorem fixed_bounded : fixed.counterexample (fun s => noZombie s && quiescentClean s) 12 = none := by
  native_decide

/-- The inductive invariant. Read as: a request runs only after its `GenerateReq` arrived and before it is
done; nothing exists before dispatch; while connected, the TokenizerManager holds exactly what it dispatched;
a departed client's dispatched request has an abort in flight or is done. -/
def inv (s : St) : Bool :=
  (!s.running || (s.dispatched && !s.genInFlight && !s.done)) &&
  (s.dispatched || (!s.genInFlight && !s.abortInFlight && !s.running && !s.done && !s.tmHas)) &&
  (!s.genInFlight || (!s.done && !s.running)) &&
  (!s.client || (s.tmHas == s.dispatched && !s.abortInFlight)) &&
  (s.client || !s.dispatched || s.abortInFlight || s.done)

def bools : List Bool := [false, true]

def allStates : List St := do
  let c ← bools; let t ← bools; let d ← bools; let g ← bools; let a ← bools; let r ← bools; let f ← bools
  pure ⟨c, t, d, g, a, r, f⟩

theorem mem_allStates (s : St) : s ∈ allStates := by
  obtain ⟨c, t, d, g, a, r, f⟩ := s
  cases c <;> cases t <;> cases d <;> cases g <;> cases a <;> cases r <;> cases f <;> native_decide

theorem inv_start : inv start = true := by decide

theorem inv_preserved :
    allStates.all (fun s => !inv s || (enabled s).all fun a => inv (stepWith disconnectFixed s a)) = true := by
  decide

theorem inv_safe : allStates.all (fun s => !inv s || (noZombie s && quiescentClean s)) = true := by
  decide

/-- For every reachable state of the fixed protocol, in every interleaving: no zombie, and clean at quiescence. -/
theorem fixed_safe (s : St) (hs : Reachable fixed s) : noZombie s = true ∧ quiescentClean s = true := by
  have hinv : inv s = true := by
    refine Reachable.inductive_invariant (sys := fixed) (fun s => inv s = true) ?_ ?_ s hs
    · intro s h
      simp [fixed] at h
      subst h
      exact inv_start
    · intro s a h ha
      have hall := List.all_eq_true.mp inv_preserved s (mem_allStates s)
      simp only [h, Bool.not_true, Bool.false_or, List.all_eq_true] at hall
      exact hall a ha
  have hsafe := List.all_eq_true.mp inv_safe s (mem_allStates s)
  simp only [hinv, Bool.not_true, Bool.false_or, Bool.and_eq_true] at hsafe
  exact hsafe

end SGLang.Behaviour

{"arguments":{"content":"# Bug classes: the shape of bugs

Code has a shape, work on it has a shape, and bugs have shapes too. A **bug class** is a mechanism: a way code goes
wrong that recurs across places and codebases. It is not a symptom. "Crash" is a symptom; "state registered
before a cancellable await, with no cleanup on that path" is a class. Classes are what can be eliminated one at a
time: find every **site** where the class can occur, and put a **guard** there, or make the site impossible.

This is the shared seed: the ids are stable across SGLang, vLLM, zml and compute, so the four maps can be compared.
Each class below was seen at least once in the defects verified by hand in rounds 1–2 (examples cited). Workers
may propose new classes, splits or merges in their own `maps/bugs/CLASS_PROPOSALS.md`, with evidence. The
orchestrator merges them here.

Each class has:
- a **mechanism**: how the bug arises;
- a **site**: the code pattern where it *can* occur, which a program should be able to find;
- a **guard**: what makes a site safe;
- **symptoms**;
- **examples**.

{"arguments":{"content":"# leanserve: an LLM serving engine in Lean 4, planned from SGLang

**The plan in one paragraph.** Rewrite SGLang's *control plane* in Lean 4:
- the API, tokenization, scheduling, KV-cache and memory management;
- configuration resolution, parsers and structured output;
- the protocols between processes.

Its core invariants are proved, not tested. Keep the *data plane* (GPU kernels and model forward passes) foreign at
first:
- **phase 1** drives SGLang's own Python model runner through a narrow batch interface;
- **phase 2** calls CUDA libraries (FlashInfer, cuBLAS, NCCL) directly through Lean's C FFI.

SGLang stays the reference implementation throughout: every stage is checked against it by differential tests.

This is where the evidence says Lean pays. 46% of SGLang's control-plane bug fixes fall in classes Lean can rule out
by construction. The data plane's bugs are mostly hardware and configuration-combination bugs, where Lean helps far
less.

Working name, repository layout and phase gates below. Nothing here is built yet.

## 1. Why this is worth doing: the evidence

The SGLang maps (`theoriclabs/sglang-fork`, branch `sglang-maps`, `maps/`) classified 600 random SGLang fixes by
bug class, twice and independently (kappa 0.73). Splitting them by where the fix landed:

| where the fix landed | fixes | share |
|---|---|---|
| control plane (`managers/`, `mem_cache/`, `entrypoints/`, config, parsers, disaggregation, sampling, constrained decoding) | 209 | 35% |
| data plane (`layers/`, `models/`, `model_executor/`, kernels, speculative decoding, distributed) | 284 | 47% |
| other (docs, tests, CI) or mixed | 107 | 18% |

Inside the control plane, by class, and what Lean does about each:

| class | control-plane fixes | what Lean does |
|---|---|---|
| copy-drift | 20 | **Rules it out.** One definition generates the CLI choice lists, docs, wire schema and dispatch. There is no second copy to drift. |
| unit-mismatch | 14 | **Rules it out.** `Tokens`, `Pages`, `Slots`, `Bytes` and per-rank against global quantities are distinct types; mixing them does not compile. |
| ordering-assumed | 13 | **Proves it,** for CPU-side ordering. The scheduler is an explicit event loop, with its ordering properties proved in a transition-system model. |
| accepted-not-honored | 9 | **Rules it out.** Resolution is a total function from arguments to a resolved configuration. Every accepted field is consumed, or the input is refused, by construction. |
| ownership-transfer | 8 | **Proves it.** KV slot ownership (free list, a request's partial page, radix tree) is a state machine with the `slotOwner` invariant proved. |
| terminal-leak | 8 | **Proves it.** The request lifecycle is a transition system: "terminal implies every resource released" is a theorem. |
| fault-uncontained | 8 | **Rules it out.** The request pipeline is total, and errors are values. One bad request cannot unwind the scheduler loop. |
| default-swallow | 7 | **Rules it out.** Registries are inductive types matched exhaustively. A new backend is a compile error at every unhandled site. |
| cross-process-agreement | 7 | **Rules it out.** Both sides of every process boundary use one Lean type for the message, and a handshake theorem covers version and configuration agreement. |
| cancel-window | 2 | **Proves it.** Cancellation points are actions in the lifecycle model; register-then-cancel is proved to clean up. That is the SGLang zombie decode (#36333) and vLLM's `n == 1` window, both found in the maps. |
| check-then-act | 1 | **Proves it:** a single owner of the scheduler state, with atomic decisions. |
| **subtotal** | **97 of 209 (46%)** | |
| untested-crossing | 15 | **Makes it explicit.** Resolution refuses any combination not in a declared support matrix (a type), so silent breakage becomes a refusal until someone adds and tests the cell. |
| none of the 17 classes | 88 | Partly: logic errors against a written specification are caught where the specification is proved. |
| platform-path, dependency-drift, numerics-drift | 9 | **Nothing.** These live at the hardware boundary. |

Caveats:
- The plane split is by file path.
- The labels have a kappa of 0.73.
- "Rules it out" means *for code written in Lean*: the guarantee ends at the FFI boundary.

Still, it is the most concrete evidence we have: **about half of what goes wrong in SGLang's control plane is the
kind of thing a dependently typed language with proofs closes by construction.**

## 2. Where it will really shine

Ranked by how much bug surface it removes and how much the proof buys.

1. **The KV cache and memory manager.** This is the radix tree, the page allocator, request-to-token rows and
   hierarchical caching.
   - Every invariant here is crisp, and SGLang's issues show them breaking: `slotOwner` 9 times, `memorySlack` 9,
     wrong accounting 18.
   - In Lean, the allocator's free list, locked and evictable nodes, and page accounting are one structure with
     proofs. No slot has two owners; a locked path is never evicted; accounting conserves.
   - SGLang already has a second implementation (the Rust `TreeCore`), so there is a precedent and an oracle.
2. **Configuration resolution.** SGLang has 515 flags, 648 env vars and 954 coupling rules today, spread across hook
   files.
   - In leanserve, resolution is one total function `resolve : Args → Hardware → Model → Except Refusal Resolved`.
   - Three things are theorems:
     - every refusal names the rule that caused it;
     - every accepted field reaches a reader;
     - every accepted combination is in the declared support matrix.
   - This removes SGLang's largest issue pattern, "accepted but not honored" (seven of ten issue batches named it),
     and turns its largest fix class, untested crossings (12%), into explicit refusals.
   - The docs and CLI are generated from the same definitions.
3. **The request lifecycle and the protocols between processes:** tokenizer, scheduler, detokenizer,
   prefill-decode transfer, abort and streaming.
   - The behaviour models from the maps (`formal/SGLang/Behaviour.lean`, compute's `Lifecycle.lean`, vLLM's
     abort model) stop being models *of* the code and become the code: the step function is the implementation.
   - Zombie decodes, leaked slots and PD mismatches become theorems about the implementation, not bugs in it.
4. **The scheduler, with no GIL.** SGLang built its overlap scheduler and a Rust HTTP server largely to hide
   Python's CPU overhead.
   - A compiled Lean scheduler (Lean 4 compiles to C, uses reference counting and updates in place) removes the
     overhead instead of hiding it.
   - Prefix matching, admission against the prefill budgets, retraction and batch assembly run as native code, with
     their fairness and budget properties stated and proved.
5. **Parsers and structured output.** SGLang has 41 tool-call parsers and 33 reasoning parsers, and grammar-
   constrained decoding.
   - Parsers written as total, streaming parser combinators, with two proofs:
     - round trip against the chat template (`parserInvertsTemplate`, an invariant SGLang's issues had to
       invent);
     - streaming prefix stability: incremental output never retracts.
   - Grammar automata with their acceptance proved against the grammar.
6. **The API edge.** OpenAI-compatible routes on `leanapi`, with typed validation and 422 errors that name the
   field.
   - A `Secret` type that has no `ToJson`, so `/server_info` cannot leak an API key. SGLang (#37457) and vLLM both
     leak today.
   - Per-request error boundaries by construction.
7. **Shape and unit discipline at the model boundary.** Batch descriptors carry tensor shapes and units in their
   types. Padding and reshaping arithmetic of the kind that broke SGLang (232 padded rows reshaped to `[38, 6, -1]`,
   5f216fc33f) is proved before a kernel is launched.
8. **The map is the code.** The SGLang maps had to build a Lean model *beside* a Python codebase and keep the two in
   sync by hand. In leanserve:
   - the shape model (components, typed edges, registries, invariants) is the program's own types;
   - the harness per project (classify a change, demand evidence, refuse the inadmissible) runs on real types,
     not a model of them;
   - every bug class with a local pattern gets a guard at the type level, checked on every change.

## 3. Where it will not shine: said plainly

- **Kernels and numerics.** Attention, GEMM, MoE, quantization and communication stay CUDA, Triton or vendor
  libraries. Lean can specify their shapes and index arithmetic, and test them differentially. It cannot prove a
  GPU kernel. That covers numerics drift, and most of the data plane's 284 fixes.
- **Hardware breadth.** SGLang runs on nine platforms. Every platform is FFI work, and platform-path bugs (10.5% of
  SGLang's fixes) are not reduced by Lean. Start with CUDA on one architecture.
- **Model breadth and day-0 support.** SGLang supports 279 architectures and ships new ones the day they release, in
  Python. leanserve will support a few families for a long time. This is SGLang's moat, and leanserve should not
  compete on it.
- **Ecosystem:** Hugging Face configs and tokenizers, 31 quantization formats, LoRA, multimodal processors. Each is
  FFI or a port.
- **Iteration speed:** Lean compile times, a small pool of engineers who know Lean, and proofs that must be
  maintained as the code changes.
- **Hot-loop performance, if done carelessly.** Boxed arrays and reference-counted objects in per-token paths.
  Per-token data must live in `ByteArray` or `FloatArray` or in foreign buffers, with in-place updates checked by
  benchmark.

**Positioning:** a verified control plane for LLM serving, with a narrow, well-typed boundary to the fastest
available kernels. It is not "SGLang but in Lean" across its full breadth.

## 4. Architecture

```
            leanapi (OpenAI-compatible HTTP, SSE, WebSocket via leanws)
                                  |
         Frontend: validation, Secret, chat templates, tokenization (FFI to HF tokenizers)
                                  |   typed IPC (one Lean type per message, both sides)
         Scheduler: event loop, admission, retraction, batch assembly  <-- proved lifecycle
                                  |
         Memory: radix tree + page allocator + request rows + HiCache tiers  <-- proved ownership
                                  |   BatchDescriptor (about 15 fields; shapes and units in the types)
   +------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
   | phase 1: Python worker process running SGLang's ModelRunner        |
   |          (builds ForwardBatch from the descriptor)                 |
   | phase 2: Lean model runner calling FlashInfer, cuBLAS, NCCL via C FFI |
   +--------------------------------------------------------------------+
         Output: detokenization (incremental, streaming-prefix proved), parsers, grammar automata
```

Module map, from SGLang's components (the maps' `Stack.lean` inventory) to Lean modules:

| SGLang | leanserve | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `http_server`, `openai/serving_*` | `Serve.Api` on leanapi | routes, SSE streaming, 422 validation |
| `tokenizer_manager`, `template_manager` | `Serve.Frontend` | tokenizers through a C FFI to the Rust `tokenizers` library; Jinja chat templates ported or through FFI |
| `server_args`, `arg_groups/*`, `environ` | `Serve.Config` | total `resolve`; rules as data; docs and CLI generated |
| `scheduler`, `schedule_policy`, `prefill_adder` | `Serve.Sched` | event loop; policies as a registry type |
| `mem_cache/radix_cache`, allocators, `req_to_token` | `Serve.Mem` | the proved core |
| `detokenizer_manager`, `function_call/`, `parser/` | `Serve.Output` | streaming detokenizer and parsers |
| `constrained/` | `Serve.Grammar` | automata with acceptance proofs |
| `disaggregation/` | `Serve.PD` (phase 3) | handshake and transfer as a proved protocol |
| `model_executor/`, `layers/`, `models/` | `Serve.Model` via FFI | phase 1: Python worker; phase 2: Lean with C FFI |

## 5. What gets proved (the theorem list, per module)

| module | theorems |
|---|---|
| `Serve.Mem` | every slot has exactly one owner; a locked path is never evicted; eviction frees only unlocked leaves; page accounting conserves; prefix matching returns the longest cached prefix |
| `Serve.Sched` | admission never exceeds any of the three prefill budgets; `max_running_requests` never exceeds the request rows; retraction restores the state it took; every admitted request eventually completes or is aborted, under a fairness assumption stated as a hypothesis |
| lifecycle | terminal implies all resources released; an abort from any state reaches the scheduler and frees the request's slots (no zombie); streaming output is prefix-stable |
| `Serve.Config` | `resolve` is total; every accepted field is read; every refusal names its rule; accepted combinations are within the support matrix |
| `Serve.Output` | parsers invert the chat template; the incremental detokenizer's output is a prefix of the final text |
| `Serve.PD` (phase 3) | prefill and decode agree on page size, KV dtype and layout before any transfer; the transfer protocol neither loses nor duplicates KV pages |
| FFI boundary | not provable. Stated as hypotheses, and checked by differential tests and runtime asserts |

## 6. What already exists to build on

- **leanapi:** routing, typed parameters, JSON and 422 validation. The API layer.
- **leanws:** WebSocket in pure Lean. Realtime and streaming transports.
- **leanhttp:** a working C FFI pattern (libcurl) and a release setup. The template for the CUDA and tokenizer FFI
  shims.
- **leanworkflow:** "prove no work is stranded" for state machines. The request lifecycle is exactly that problem.
- **The SGLang maps' Lean** (`maps/formal/`):
  - the component and registry types;
  - the 954 extracted rules (`Catalog.lean`), which seed `Serve.Config`'s rule data;
  - the behaviour-model pattern.
- **SGLang itself:** the reference implementation, the source of the model runner in phase 1, and the benchmark
  scripts (`bench_serving`).

## 7. Phases, each with a gate

| phase | builds | gate (must pass to continue) |
|---|---|---|
| **0. Spec** (2 weeks) | `Serve.Mem` and the lifecycle as pure Lean with proofs; `Serve.Config` resolving a subset (about 60 flags for dense models) | theorems in §5 for these modules proved with no `sorry`; `resolve` matches SGLang's resolved config on 200 real launch commands from the issue corpus |
| **1. Verified brain, borrowed muscle** (6–8 weeks) | frontend, scheduler and memory in Lean; a Python worker process running SGLang's `ModelRunner` behind a `BatchDescriptor` over shared memory; one model family (Llama or Qwen3 dense), one GPU | greedy outputs token-identical to SGLang on a 1,000-request conformance corpus; throughput within 10% of SGLang, and time-to-first-token no worse at p50 and p99; scheduler CPU time per step measured against SGLang's |
| **2. Own the data plane** (8–12 weeks) | Lean model runner over C FFI to FlashInfer, cuBLAS and NCCL; CUDA graphs; tensor parallelism | the same conformance at TP = 1, 2, 4; throughput within 10% of SGLang; no Python in the serving path |
| **3. Distinctive features** | prefill-decode disaggregation (proved protocol), speculative decoding (proved acceptance logic), structured output (proved automata), HiCache tiers | each feature's theorems proved, and differential conformance against SGLang for the same feature |
| **4. Breadth, driven by demand** | more model families, quantization formats, a second platform | per addition: conformance, and a support-matrix cell declared |

## 8. How it is tested

- **Differential conformance against SGLang:**
  - a corpus of requests × configurations × seeds;
  - greedy outputs must be token-identical, and sampled outputs identical under the same seed and sampler;
  - streaming event sequences are compared too.
- **Property tests at the FFI boundary:** everything a theorem assumes about foreign code is asserted at run time in
  debug builds.
- **Benchmarks:** SGLang's `bench_serving` against both engines on the same GPU, same model and same request trace.
- **The maps' harness on itself:** leanserve's own changes are classified and gated with the same operation
  vocabulary.

## 9. Risks

| risk | mitigation |
|---|---|
| Lean runtime overhead in per-token paths | per-token data in unboxed arrays and foreign buffers; benchmark gate at phase 1 |
| The phase-1 seam is awkward: `ForwardBatch` has 106 fields | a descriptor covering the dense-model core (about 15 fields), with the Python worker filling defaults; scope limited to dense models in phase 1 |
| Proof maintenance slows iteration | proofs only where §1 shows bug surface; everything else typed but unproved |
| The FFI boundary is where bugs move to | narrow, typed boundary; runtime asserts on every foreign call; differential tests |
| Tokenizer and chat-template fidelity | FFI to the Rust `tokenizers` library; template output compared byte for byte with SGLang's |
| Scope creep toward SGLang's breadth | positioning in §3; the support matrix refuses what is not declared |

{"arguments":{"file_path":"/Users/harshwork/code/leanserve/PLAN.md","new_string":"## 3. What stays hard, even with lowering

- **Matching hand-tuned kernel speed.** FlashInfer, CUTLASS and FlashMLA encode years of per-architecture tricks:
  warp specialisation, TMA, `wgmma`, register-level pipelining. A generated kernel is only as fast as its schedule.
  The schedule language must expose these tricks, and its search must find good schedules. Until it does, lowering
  can target the libraries themselves (generate the calls, prove the layouts), with generated kernels only where
  they win.
- **Floating-point proofs.** Rewrites are cheap to prove in exact arithmetic. Bounding their floating-point error is
  expensive, so it is reserved for the few kernels where drift has bitten: fused paths, low-precision accumulation.
  Everything else is equivalence in exact arithmetic plus differential tests.
- **The trusted base grows.** The lowering (Lean to CUDA, Triton or Rust) is unverified, and so are nvcc, the Triton
  compiler and the drivers. The mitigations:
  - translation validation on every generated artifact, with each output compared to the Lean reference;
  - later, proofs for the generator's layout and index core, as Fiat Cryptography did for field arithmetic.
- **Model and ecosystem breadth.** SGLang supports 279 architectures, 31 quantization formats, LoRA and multimodal
  processors. Lowering makes each port *checkable*, not free. Agent-drafted model specifications help with the
  volume.
- **Iteration speed:** Lean compile times, a small pool of engineers who know Lean, and proofs that must be
  maintained as the code changes.
- **Hot paths in the Lean runtime**, where Lean is the runtime: per-token data belongs in unboxed arrays or foreign
  buffers. Where this bites, lower that module to Rust or C instead.

**Positioning:** one proved specification of an LLM serving engine, lowered to the best host language for each layer
and each platform. The control plane is proved outright. Kernels get proved algorithms and layouts with validated
schedules. SGLang is the oracle, and a first customer for the lowered pieces.","old_string":"## 3. Where it will not shine: said plainly

  maintained as the code changes.

{"arguments":{"file_path":"/Users/harshwork/code/leanserve/PLAN.md","new_string":"### 4.1 The kernel database and selection

Kernels, the instances they run on, machines and measurements are strongly typed LeanDB tables. A sketch, in
LeanDB's style:

```lean
inductive Op      where | rmsnorm | rope | gemm | pagedAttnDecode | prefillAttn | moeGroupedGemm | quantFp8 | allReduce
  deriving Repr, DecidableEq, Ord, LeanDb.ClosedEnum
inductive Backend where | flashinfer | cutlass | deepgemm | triton | cuteDsl | aiter | generated
  deriving Repr, DecidableEq, Ord, LeanDb.ClosedEnum
inductive Arch    where | sm80 | sm90 | sm100 | sm120 | gfx942 | gfx950
  deriving Repr, DecidableEq, Ord, LeanDb.ClosedEnum

structure Kernel where
  op        : Op
  backend   : Backend
  version   : Version        -- library version, or the generator commit for generated kernels
  target    : Target         -- a library entry point, or a generated artifact
  applies   : Applicability  -- dtypes, architectures, shape constraints (ranges, divisibility), required features
  numerics  : Numerics       -- bitExact | batchInvariant | withinTolerance ε
  deriving Repr, LeanDb.Entity

structure Instance where     -- one shape bucket of one op
  op : Op;  dtype : DType;  m : Bucket;  n : Nat;  k : Nat;  features : FeatureSet
  deriving Repr, LeanDb.Entity

structure Machine where
  arch : Arch;  gpu : GpuModel;  driver : Version;  libs : LibVersions
  deriving Repr, LeanDb.Entity

structure Measurement where
  kernel  : Ref Kernel
  inst    : Ref Instance
  machine : Ref Machine
  p50     : Micros
  p95     : Micros
  maxErr  : ErrorBound       -- against the Lean reference for this op
  runs    : Nat
  harness : Version
  deriving Repr, LeanDb.Entity

structure TunedConfig where  -- replaces SGLang's per-GPU JSON files
  kernel : Ref Kernel;  bucket : Ref Instance;  machine : Ref Machine;  tiles : TileConfig
  deriving Repr, LeanDb.Entity
```

**Selection is a query that returns a proof.** `select inst machine policy` has five steps:
1. join `Kernel` and `Measurement` for this instance and machine;
2. keep the kernels whose `applies` is *decided* true for the instance and machine, and whose `numerics` meets the
   policy (deterministic mode requires `batchInvariant`, strict mode `bitExact`);
3. keep only measurements whose kernel version and harness are current;
4. take the one with the lowest `p50`, or `p95` for latency service levels;
5. return the kernel together with the proof that it applies.

When nothing applies:
- **strict mode:** the instance is refused;
- **otherwise:** it falls back to the reference, with a warning.

Four theorems follow:
